title: 1. Aggregate Trends
text:
Investment in research and development (R&D) – activities to generate new knowledge and create new technology – is a cornerstone input for innovation. This report provides an update of major global trends in R&D and related innovation metrics across the major R&D economies, with a focus on American competitiveness. This report relies primarily on new data from the Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), 1the Web of Science’s publication archives, 2 and the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO). 3 All sources are cited at the bottom of each figure for clarity of origin.

#### 1. Aggregate Trends

Adjusted for inflation and cross-economy price differences, global R&D investment has tripled over the past 30 years, from $672 billion in 1992 to over $2.2 trillion as of 2021, as can be seen in figure 1.1. Last year’s report attempted to correct for the then absence of Chinese data, which has been vetted and included in this latest version – hitting the mark expected for 2021.

In last year’s report, it was noted that OECD countries, which make up thirty-eight of the world’s most wealthy and robust economies, are no longer the sole drivers of R&D globally. This trend continues, with China, the largest non OECD economy reporting R&D funding, contributing 27% of R&D investments globally in 2021, and representing 98% of non-OECD investments. The U.S. remains the top spender, funding 32% of global R&D in 2021.

R&D funding as a share of GDP has plateaued for the OECD countries at large – staying at about 2.7% from 2020 to 2022, ashown as the dotted line and right-side axis of the figure. A plateau overall does not mean that all countries are plateauing (more on that in the next section) nor are all sectors behaving the same way.

## U.S. R&D and Innovation in a Global Context:

### The 2024 Data Update

ALESSANDRA ZIMMERMANN | APRIL 23 2024

BOTTOM LINE: The U.S. remains the largest R&D spender, but that is its only 1 st place in 2022. The U.S. is 4 th in total R&D intensity, 12 th in government R&D intensity, 5 thin basic science intensity and 14 th in number of researchers adjusted for labor force. China publishes more and applies for more PCT patents than the U.S. China has more researchers, and has promised more R&D investments.

a 2022 is not shown on the graph due to the absence of data from China that skews the world total significantly.

The business sector, as seen in Figure 1.2, is by far the largest funder of R&D in the OECD economies, providing over $1.07 trillion and accounting for 63% of OECD R&D in 2022. That year, government financing – which refers almost entirely to national government in most cases – accounted for 22% of R&D, and the remainder was composed of universities, nonprofits, and foreign sources.

However, since 1992, relative funding growth has looked somewhat different (figure 1.3). Over that time, R&D funding from higher education and other nonprofit institutions more than tripled in real terms (227% increase over 28 years), and finally shook off a plateau incurred by the pandemic from 2019 to 2021. In that same period business R&D financing has more than doubled (180% increase), with a recent spike in growth from 2021 to 2022 (an 8% year over year funding increase). Government R&D has only increased by 64% over that same period of time, and with only a 0.4% increase in funding from 2021 to 2022. Stagnant government funding is not new to OECD economies who have seen a mere 15% increase since the financial crisis in 2009 – that is an

average of 1% increase per year, and most of that jump happened between 2016 and 2018.

The graphs show data over the first years of the pandemic; note that the business sector sustained increases in R&D, and higher-education and non-profit sectors increased after a plateau during the initial years of the pandemic. Government-funded R&D saw a spike up for 2020 and 2021 but stayed level in 2022. Level funding is not necessarily bad; it implies that some R&D funding from the pandemic appears to be sticking around instead of returning to pre-pandemic levels. More on individual countries’ funding patterns will be discussed in the next section.

#### 2. R&D Investments by Country: U.S. Remains top Funder, Slows in Public R&D Intensity

This section looks at total investment in R&D per country, adding up private (business), public (government) and other sources (higher education and philanthropy among others) to compile a profile of R&D funding for each country, reported to the OECD. China is reporting the largest growth in R&D expenditure of any country, followed by Korea and Taiwan, as can be seen in figure 2.1. All three countries have made R&D a national priority, writing specific fields into their policies. 4,5,6 The U.S. remains in 5 th place, with an average annual growth in R&D expenditure at 3.8%.

As can be seen in figure 2.2, the U.S. is still the largest spender on R&D in the world, though China did not report 2022 numbers. The U.S. and other nations are seeing a decrease in the rate of R&D funding as emergency pandemic work eased, with only Korea and Japan having a larger percent increase during 2021 to 2022 as compared to 2020 to 2021. In Korea, this is in part thanks to an increase in federal funding approved by the Korean Presidential Advisory Council of Science and Technology 7, as well as the continued rollout of tax incentives to encourage business R&D. The rest of the world’s countries as a sum also saw a larger percent increase than the previous year, recovering from the drop in R&D funding seen in 2020-2021. R&D Intensity: R&D intensity – or R&D as a share of gross domestic product – indicates the relative share of resources devoted to R&D in an economy, providing an indicator of its innovative capacity. For instance, Israel and Korea, the two countries with the most R&D-intensive economies, spend far less on R&D than the United States or China in absolute dollars, but those dollars account for a much larger share of their respective economies, indicating stronger relative focus on science and innovation.

The U.S. is now climbing its way back up the rankings after dropping out of the top five in the mid-1990s. In 2022, the U.S. retained its spot in 4 th place in R&D intensity. Israel, Korea, and Taiwan, respectively, remain at the top, while the U.S. crept ahead of Germany in 2019, and more recently outpaced Japan and Sweden (figure 2.3). China was expected to continue its dramatic rise upwards, with a goal towards 3% of GDP, but reached 2.4% in 2021, the last data point reported to the OECD. Public and Private R&D Intensity. Not every economy portions out its research the same way, with some countries favoring government or private sector investments in R&D. Focusing first on public R&D intensity in figure 2.4, the U.S. has fallen in the leadership ranks since the 1990s, placing 12 th in 2021, behind Korea and a selection of European countries. The U.S. federal contribution stayed the same between 2021 and 2022, returning to pre pandemic levels with 0.65%. Act in 2023 this same pattern will likely continue for U.S. funding. Korea, the leader in public spending, also announced austerity measures that would cut future R&D funding in 2023, 9though some of that cut may still be walked back. In terms of reported data, Korea remains one of the largest proportional funders of R&D, along with Norway, who saw a significant dip in federal funding after an upheaval of its research funding agency. 10 Thanks to this decrease, Germany, Austria, and Switzerland overtook Norway for second through fourth place, respectively, in 2021. China saw a slight decrease in public spending in 2021, though that is expected to change in the coming years with their declarations of significant investments in R&D in 2024. 11

While public funding decreased post-pandemic, the same cannot be said of private funding which continues to increase in intensity, as is shown in figure 2.5. The only major R&D economy that saw a decrease in private R&D funding was Austria, while others saw sharp increases like Japan and Korea, who once again tops the chart. Many of the countries that saw private R&D funding increases are doing so through tax reforms that attract innovation-heavy industries, Korea expensing tax benefits in 2016, or through foreign direct investments as is the case of Taiwan and Israel. The U.S. dropped one rank in 2021 to 5 th in private R&D intensity, Israel reclaiming its 4 th place. The U.S. passed several bills in 2022, most notably the Inflation Reduction Act, which contain tax incentives for private R&D efforts and the results of which we may start to see in next year’s data. Basic Science Intensity. In the same way that different economies feature differing mixes of funding sources, they can also exhibit a tendency toward short-term investment by focusing on development spending or toward longer-term investment through basic science. Basic science is inherently uncertain with unpredictable results, and the gap between initial investment and economic impact can amount to several years, if ever. 12 The tangible benefits from knowledge gains can also be difficult for individual investors to recoup due to knowledge spillovers.
